title: Reading Genealogies and Lists
summary: Why the Bible keeps records of names and numbers: how ancient genealogies worked and what they did for their first readers, the genealogies of Genesis, Chronicles, Matthew, and Luke, the large numbers and the debates over them, the other lists of Scripture, and what a modern reader can learn from them.

sections.body:
Many readers who set out to read the Bible from the beginning are stopped by the lists: the long line of ‘and he lived, and he had sons and daughters, and he died’ in Genesis 5, the nations of Genesis 10, the census of Numbers 1 and 26, the boundary lists of Joshua, and above all the nine chapters of names that open 1 Chronicles. The New Testament begins with one: “This is the record of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham” (Matthew 1:1). It is tempting to skip them. But they are there on purpose, and their first readers would not have skipped them at all.

In the ancient world a genealogy was not a hobby or a curiosity. It was a claim. It said who a person was, to whom he belonged, what he could inherit, what offices he could hold, and which promises applied to him. Land in Israel was divided by tribe and clan and passed down within families (Numbers 26:52-56), so a family line was also a title deed. Priesthood belonged to the descendants of Aaron, and after the exile some men who claimed to be priests “searched for their family records, but they could not find them and so were excluded from the priesthood” (Ezra 2:62). Kingship in Judah belonged to the house of David. The first-century historian Josephus opens his autobiography by setting out his own priestly descent, which he says he found recorded in the public registers (Life 1-6). Names in a list were how a community remembered who it was.

There is also a theological reason. The Bible's story is about promises made to particular people and passed down through generations: to Eve that her offspring would crush the serpent's head (Genesis 3:15), to Abraham that through his offspring all nations would be blessed (Genesis 22:18), to David that his house and kingdom would endure (2 Samuel 7:16). A genealogy traces how those promises were carried, often through unlikely people and across long silences, from one generation to the next. When the lists slow a reader down, they are also saying: God keeps his word over centuries, through ordinary people whose names are mostly all we know of them.

The most important study of the subject in English is Robert R. Wilson's Genealogy and History in the Biblical World (1977), which compared biblical genealogies with those of other ancient Near Eastern peoples and with genealogies recorded by anthropologists in modern tribal societies. Several of his observations have become standard.

Genealogies come in two main shapes. A linear genealogy traces a single line from one person to a descendant, one name per generation, as in Genesis 5 from Adam to Noah or Ruth 4:18-22 from Perez to David. Its purpose is usually to connect a later person to an earlier one and so to establish his right or standing. A segmented genealogy branches, listing several children in each generation and following different lines, as in the table of nations in Genesis 10 or the tribal lists in Chronicles. Its purpose is usually to describe relationships among groups, who is close kin and who is distant.

Genealogies also serve different functions in different spheres of life, domestic, political and legal, and religious, and they change shape according to their function. The same family might be recorded one way for inheritance and another for worship. Genealogies can be fluid: names are dropped, merged, or added as circumstances change, and lines are often shortened by leaving out generations that do not matter to the point being made. In ancient usage ‘son of’ can mean grandson or descendant, and ‘father of’ can mean ancestor. Matthew calls Jesus ‘the son of David, the son of Abraham’ in a single breath.

This means that biblical genealogies should not be read as modern family trees, complete and precise in every generation. They are selective, often arranged in patterns (ten generations, fourteen generations), and shaped to make a point. That is not a flaw. It is how genealogies worked everywhere in the ancient world, and a reader who knows it will not be troubled that two genealogies of the same line differ, and will look instead for why each was shaped as it was.

Genesis is built on genealogy. Its main sections are introduced by a recurring heading, the Hebrew toledot, ‘generations’, rendered in the Berean Standard Bible “This is the account of” and in older versions ‘These are the generations of’. The first comes after the creation account, “This is the account of the heavens and the earth when they were created” (Genesis 2:4), and the last introduces the story of Joseph (37:2). The structure moves from the whole world to one family: after each account the book sets aside the lines that do not carry the promise (Cain, Ishmael, Esau) with a brief genealogy, and then follows the chosen line in detail.

Genesis 5 traces ten generations from Adam to Noah, each with the same formula: when X had lived so many years he fathered Y, then lived so many more years and had other sons and daughters, and he died. The refrain ‘and then he died’, repeated eight times, is a steady drumbeat after the warning of Genesis 2:17. It is broken once, for Enoch: “Enoch walked with God, and then he was no more, because God had taken him away.” (5:24). Genesis 11:10-26 gives a matching ten-generation line from Shem to Abram, with lifespans that shrink generation by generation. Genesis 10, the table of nations, lists the descendants of Noah's three sons as the peoples of the known world. It names seventy nations in the Hebrew text (seventy-two in the Septuagint), and many interpreters connect this to the seventy (or seventy-two, in some manuscripts) disciples whom Jesus sends out in Luke 10:1.

The long lifespans of Genesis 5, Methuselah's 969 years among them, have been read in several ways. Many readers take them literally, as the natural lifespans of humanity before the flood. Others note that ancient Mesopotamian tradition also gave enormous figures to the earliest rulers: the Sumerian King List assigns the kings before the flood reigns of tens of thousands of years each. Some scholars think the biblical numbers are deliberately modest by comparison and carry symbolic value; others have proposed specific numerical schemes; others take them as honorific. The numbers also differ among the ancient textual traditions. The Septuagint usually adds a hundred years to a patriarch's age at the birth of his son, and the Samaritan Pentateuch has its own figures, so that the total from Adam to the flood comes to 1,656 years in the Masoretic Text, 1,307 in the Samaritan Pentateuch, and 2,242 in the Septuagint. The Septuagint also includes an extra generation, Cainan, between Arphaxad and Shelah in Genesis 11, and Luke's genealogy follows it (Luke 3:36).

Can the genealogies be added up to date creation? In 1650 Archbishop James Ussher, using the Hebrew figures, dated creation to 4004 BC, and his dates were printed in the margins of many English Bibles for two centuries. In 1890 the Princeton Old Testament scholar William Henry Green published an article on primeval chronology arguing that the genealogies of Genesis 5 and 11, like other biblical genealogies, may omit generations and were never intended as a chronology; B. B. Warfield agreed. Young-earth creationists maintain that the genealogies are complete, or nearly so, and give a timescale of thousands of years. Most other interpreters, conservative and critical, follow Green in holding that the lists were not designed for adding up. The question belongs with the larger debate about the days of Genesis, set out in the introduction to Genesis in this Study Bible.

sections.h: Chronicles: who we are after the exile
sections.body:
The longest genealogy in the Bible fills the first nine chapters of 1 Chronicles. It begins, with no introduction at all, “Adam, Seth, Enosh” (1 Chronicles 1:1), and runs through the nations and the patriarchs to the twelve tribes of Israel, with special attention to Judah and the house of David, to Levi and the priests, and to Benjamin, the tribes that made up the community after the exile. It ends by stating the reason for the history that follows: “So all Israel was recorded in the genealogies written in the Book of the Kings of Israel. But Judah was exiled to Babylon because of their unfaithfulness.” (9:1), and then lists those who resettled in Jerusalem.

Chronicles was written for the community that returned from Babylon to a small, poor province of the Persian Empire, most likely in the fourth century BC. They had lost their king, their independence, and most of their land. The genealogies told them that they were still the Israel that went back to Adam, still the people of the promises, still connected to the tribes and the house of David, and that the temple they served was the continuation of the worship David had organized. For such a community, a list of names was a statement of identity and hope.

The lists are also punctuated by small stories. The most famous is Jabez, who “was more honorable than his brothers” and prayed that God would bless him and keep him from harm, “And God granted the request of Jabez.” (4:9-10). In 2000 a best-selling book by Bruce Wilkinson, The Prayer of Jabez, turned these verses into a daily formula for blessing. Many commentators noted that the passage, in its setting, is a note in a family record honoring a man whose name sounded like the Hebrew word for pain and whose prayer was that the pain his name recalled would not define him, and cautioned against lifting a line out of a genealogy into a technique. It is a good example of how the small stories in the lists are worth reading, and of how they are best read where they stand.

Ezra and Nehemiah contain similar lists. The list of those who returned from exile appears in both Ezra 2 and Nehemiah 7, with a number of differences in names and figures between the two copies, and in both the individual entries add up to less than the total stated at the end. Scholars suggest copying errors in numbers (which were easily miswritten), the inclusion in the total of groups not itemized, or different stages of the record. Nehemiah 3 lists who built each section of Jerusalem's wall, household by household, and Nehemiah 7:5 shows why such records mattered: Nehemiah found “the genealogical register of those who had first returned” and used it to repopulate the city.

Two Gospels give Jesus' genealogy, and they are strikingly different. Matthew places his at the very start, running forward from Abraham to Jesus, in three sections: “In all, then, there were fourteen generations from Abraham to David, fourteen from David to the exile to Babylon, and fourteen from the exile to the Christ.” (Matthew 1:17). To reach fourteen in the second section Matthew leaves out names; comparing his list with 1 Chronicles 3 shows that three kings, Ahaziah, Joash, and Amaziah, are omitted between Joram and Uzziah (Matthew 1:8), and Jehoiakim is omitted before Jeconiah. That was an accepted practice, as Wilson's work shows, and Matthew's readers would have seen the pattern as the point. Many interpreters note that in Hebrew, where letters serve as numbers, the consonants of David's name (d-w-d) add up to fourteen, so that the whole genealogy is stamped with David's number, though others doubt Matthew intended it. Three times fourteen is also six sevens, so that Jesus begins the seventh seven, a pattern some interpreters find significant.

Matthew's genealogy also does something no other biblical genealogy does in this way: it names four women besides Mary. They are Tamar (1:3), Rahab and Ruth (1:5), and “Uriah’s wife” (1:6), Bathsheba, named only by her husband. Interpreters have offered several explanations. Jerome thought they were included as sinners, to show that Christ came for sinners; but Ruth is not portrayed as a sinner, and Tamar is called more righteous than Judah (Genesis 38:26). Many modern interpreters note that all four were outsiders or were associated with foreigners: Tamar and Rahab Canaanites, Ruth a Moabite, Bathsheba the wife of a Hittite, anticipating a Messiah for the nations, whose Gospel ends with the command to make disciples of all nations. Raymond Brown (The Birth of the Messiah, 1977) emphasized that each was part of an irregular or scandalous union through which God nonetheless carried forward the line of promise, preparing for the irregular circumstances of Jesus' own birth. These explanations can be combined. The genealogy also changes its formula at the end: instead of ‘Jacob was the father of Joseph’, it says “Jacob the father of Joseph, the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus” (1:16), where ‘of whom’ in Greek is feminine, pointing to Mary alone and preparing for the account of the virgin birth that follows.

Luke places his genealogy after Jesus' baptism, where the voice from heaven has just called Jesus God's Son, and runs it backward from Jesus through David and Abraham all the way to “the son of Adam, the son of God” (Luke 3:38). The next scene is Jesus' temptation in the wilderness. Luke's point is that Jesus belongs not only to Israel but to all humanity, a new Adam, the Son of God who will stand where the first son of God fell.

The two lists agree from Abraham to David, but between David and Joseph they differ almost completely: Matthew follows the royal line through Solomon, and Luke a line through another son of David, Nathan; Matthew names Joseph's father as Jacob, Luke as Heli (Luke 3:23). Christians have explained the difference in several ways since the early centuries. Julius Africanus, in a letter to Aristides in the early third century preserved by Eusebius (Church History 1.7), proposed that Jacob and Heli were half-brothers with the same mother, and that when Heli died childless Jacob married his widow under the law of levirate marriage (Deuteronomy 25:5-6), so that Joseph was Jacob's son by birth and Heli's by law. Another view, widely held since the late Middle Ages, is that Luke gives Mary's line, with Heli as Mary's father and Joseph named as his son-in-law; Luke's phrasing that Jesus “was regarded as the son of Joseph” (3:23) is sometimes cited in support. A third view holds that Matthew traces the legal line of royal succession and Luke the physical descent. Many critical scholars, Brown among them, think the two genealogies arose independently and cannot be fully harmonized, and that each should be read for its own theological purpose. Whichever view a reader takes, both Gospels agree on the points they were written to make: Jesus is the son of David and of Abraham, the heir of the promises, and his birth came about by God's own act.

The Bible's lists include many numbers, and some of them raise real questions. The census of Numbers 1 counts the fighting men of Israel at the start of the wilderness period: “all those counted totaled 603,550” (Numbers 1:46). With women, children, and older men, that implies a population of two million or more, which some readers find hard to reconcile with the resources of the Sinai and with other passages that describe Israel as small (Deuteronomy 7:7).

Interpreters have taken several approaches. Many take the numbers as they stand and point to the miraculous provision the story itself describes. Others note that the Hebrew word for thousand, eleph, can also mean a clan or a military unit. The Egyptologist Flinders Petrie proposed in 1906 that the census figures should be read in this light, George Mendenhall developed the idea in a 1958 article on the census lists of Numbers 1 and 26, and the Cambridge physicist Colin Humphreys offered a mathematical version in Vetus Testamentum in 1998, arriving at about five thousand fighting men. Critics of this approach point out that the Pentateuch's own totals add the units as thousands, and that Numbers 3:43-50 fits the large figures. Still others, such as David Fouts in a 1997 article, have argued that the large numbers are hyperbolic, a known convention in ancient Near Eastern royal inscriptions for expressing greatness. The debate is open, and scholars who share a high view of Scripture take each of these views.

Numbers were also especially vulnerable in copying, since small marks distinguished them, and parallel passages sometimes differ. The census David ordered is given different totals in 2 Samuel 24:9 and 1 Chronicles 21:5; 1 Kings 6:1 puts the building of the temple 480 years after the exodus, while the Septuagint says 440; Exodus 12:40 gives Israel's stay in Egypt as 430 years, while the Septuagint and Samaritan Pentateuch include the patriarchs' time in Canaan within the same figure, and Paul counts 430 years from the promise to the law (Galatians 3:17). The regnal years of the kings of Israel and Judah, with their cross-references from one kingdom to the other, were long thought impossible to reconcile until Edwin Thiele (The Mysterious Numbers of the Hebrew Kings, 1951) showed that most of the difficulties dissolve once one allows for co-regencies and for different ways of counting a king's first year; the guide to the kings of Israel and Judah uses this work. Numbers in the Bible deserve careful attention, and the honest reader will expect some puzzles.

Genealogies and censuses are not the only lists. Numbers 33 records every stage of Israel's route from Egypt to the plains of Moab, a travel itinerary that Moses recorded “At the LORD’s command” (Numbers 33:2), and scholars have compared it with Egyptian and Assyrian military itineraries. Joshua 13 to 21 sets out the boundaries and towns of each tribe, the Promised Land surveyed and distributed parcel by parcel, turning a promise made to Abraham into property lines. Lists of officials (1 Kings 4), David's mighty warriors (2 Samuel 23:8-39; 1 Chronicles 11), the temple musicians and gatekeepers (1 Chronicles 23 to 26), and the returned exiles all record that particular people served and mattered. 2 Samuel's list of David's warriors ends with Uriah the Hittite (23:39), the last name placed where the reader cannot miss it.

The New Testament has its lists too. The Twelve are named four times, in slightly different order (Matthew 10:2-4; Mark 3:16-19; Luke 6:14-16; Acts 1:13). Romans 16 greets more than two dozen people by name, women and men, Jews and Gentiles, slaves and free, and gives a glimpse of the actual membership of the church in Rome. Hebrews 11 is a roll call of faith. Even the vision of the new Jerusalem includes a list, gates inscribed with the names of the twelve tribes and foundations with the names of the twelve apostles (Revelation 21:12-14).

The New Testament also warns against misusing genealogies. Paul tells Timothy to charge certain teachers not to “devote themselves to myths and endless genealogies, which promote speculation” (1 Timothy 1:4), and Titus to avoid “foolish controversies, genealogies, arguments, and quarrels about the law” (Titus 3:9). Scholars debate what these genealogies were, whether Jewish speculative expansions of the Old Testament lines or early forms of the elaborate lists of spiritual beings later found in Gnostic systems; Irenaeus applied the warning to the Gnostics. Either way, the warning concerns genealogy used for speculation or pride of descent, not the genealogies of Scripture themselves. Hebrews makes an argument from the absence of a genealogy: Melchizedek appears in Genesis “Without father or mother or genealogy” (Hebrews 7:3), and so becomes a picture of a priesthood that does not depend on descent from Aaron.

A reader does not need to linger equally over every name, but the lists reward a different kind of attention from narrative. Ask first where the list stands and what it connects: what comes before and after it, and what line it traces. Ask what it includes and what it leaves out, and whether it has a pattern (ten generations, fourteen, twelve tribes), because the pattern often carries the meaning. Watch for the breaks in the formula, such as Enoch in Genesis 5, the four women in Matthew 1, and Jabez in 1 Chronicles 4, since that is where the writer pauses to say something. Compare parallel lists, not to catch errors but to see what each writer was doing. And notice the names that recur elsewhere in the story, since a genealogy is often a map of the whole book.

Then consider what the lists say about God and about people. They say that God works through generations, not only through heroes, and that most of the people through whom he kept his promises are remembered only by a name. They say that the story of salvation is a family story, full of irregular and unlikely people, including foreigners and sinners, and that God's purposes are not derailed by the failures in the line. They say that individuals matter: the Bible bothers to record the names of wall builders and gatekeepers, and the New Testament ends with a vision of a multitude from “every nation and tribe and people and tongue” (Revelation 7:9) before a God who knows each by name. The genealogy of Jesus, with its outsiders and its scandals, makes the same point in its own way: the family of God is formed by grace, not by pedigree.
